dataset_family: Community sample from five residential communities in Wuhan, recruited by the School of Nursing, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (derivation Dec 2020 - Jun 2021; external validation Jun - Jul 2022); not public
method_family: Single-task vs three dual-task (counting backwards, serial 7s, naming animals) timed 10 m gait, video-counted steps over the middle 6 m (speed, cadence, stride length, dual-task cost); logistic-regression diagnostic model with ROC and external validation
what_it_shows: Yang et al. 2024, Arch Phys Med Rehabil 105:930-938 (derivation sample: 62 CN vs 62 MCI per Table 1). Single-task gait already separates MCI from CN on speed (1.11 vs 0.95 m/s, p<.001) and stride length (1.22 vs 1.08 m, p<.001). Only cadence dissociates: single-task 109.55 vs 105.78 steps/min, p = .077, versus p<.001 under all three dual tasks (e.g. serial 7s 99.81 vs 86.83). The study's headline result is a dual-task (serial 7s) gait-speed model, AUC 0.906 derivation and 0.913 external.
why: Identity: PDF title, authors (Yang M, Wang Y, Tian C, Liu H, Yang Q, Hu X, Liu W) and DOI 10.1016/j.apmr.2023.12.008 match the block; extract read in full to the reference list. PART SHOWN: dual-task cadence separates MCI from CN where single-task cadence does not, which is one gait parameter out of three. WHY ONLY PARTLY, AND WEAK: (1) For the principal outcome (gait speed) and for stride length the unloaded counterpart does separate strongly (p<.001). The authors state 'Significant differences were observed in gait speed, stride length and DTC of gait speed ... across all 4 tasks', and that DT gait speed showed 'higher sensitivity than in ST', which is a matter of degree. For the dual-task limb this study therefore mostly shows 'dual task is more sensitive', which runs against the statement's 'where the static measure does not'. The cadence split is a table-level observation, neither claimed nor tested by the authors. A strict reader could score this 'no'. (2) The comparator is not matched. The MCI group is older (74.02 vs 71.65, p=.013), has more women (p=.047), is shorter (p=.010) and is less educated (p<.001), and the Table 3 group tests are unadjusted t or Mann-Whitney tests. Height and age both affect cadence, so the marginal single-task cadence null (p=.077) may be confounded in either direction. (3) There is no task-by-group interaction test for cadence; dual-task cost was computed for speed only. (4) Group sizes are inconsistent: the abstract says 69 CN / 65 MCI, while the Methods and Table 1 say 62 / 62. (5) Case-control design with convenience sampling. Glyphs: the Elsevier extract renders the plus-minus sign as a section sign (the paper's 'M§SD' convention) and table superscripts as 'y'; I decoded them and the verdict does not depend on them. INDEPENDENCE: the parent institution (HUST Tongji Medical College; author Qing Yang is in the Tongji Hospital nursing department) is shared with current supporter P-666 (Tongji Hospital neurology metabolic-syndrome clinic cohort, Feb - Nov 2024). There are no shared authors, and the cohort, recruitment route and period differ, so the sample is not the same. No overlap with any other supporter or candidate. METHOD FAMILY CAVEAT: single- vs dual-task timed gait is the same method family as the Guangzhou single/dual-task TUG in P-665/P-687, so even if admitted it would not add a distinct method family. Not a registry duplicate stub. Peer-reviewed, not a preprint. NARROWED: the packet says the record is not a convergence, so n/a.

quotes.quote: Signiﬁcant differences were observed in gait speed, stride length and DTC of gait speed between the cognitively normal and MCI group across all 4 tasks.
gait speed in DT showed higher sensitivity than in ST or DTC of gait speed.

In the derivation sample, the MCI group had a higher percentage of women and showed characteristics of older age, shorter stature, lower education level, and lower overall MMSE and MoCA scores compared to the cognitively normal group (table 1).
The t test or Mann-Whitney test was used for continuous variables to compare 2 groups according to data distribution assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
